# **Post-Vibe coding reflection:why smooth experiences do not lead to more creative outcomes**

## **How I utilized Vibe Coding and it’s inherently flawed process to visualize my commute.**

## **Optimization and Smoothness**

Everyone calls AI the word of the 2020s. I want to throw another into the ring: optimization. It’s the horse-and-carrot, the thing you chase forever and never quite catch.There’s no need to think about anything. It’s all been optimized for you. With gallons of data flowing to UX researchers and data scientists, you don’t need to decide what you’re going to do; it’s planned before you even think it. Now with LLMs, if you thought you weren’t thinking then, get ready to think even less.

Designers can’t seem to get enough of it, and now every job posting asks for these skills. Every LinkedIn post I see from designers I follow includes a tutorial or project they built. From Claude Code to Bolt, vibecoding is all the rage. Your grandma can build apps in her living room while baking cookies. Meanwhile, a skill your parents and uncles pushed you toward five years ago now feels like a string of words.

Video example of the project

Access to building digital products has dropped dramatically in the last two years. I’m a designer first, coder second, and I lean on that coding background because I like static things. Speculative design is not enough; I want to see the real thing in motion. So when these tools showed up, my curiosity kicked in.

## **The Commute That Sparked the Project**

Press enter or click to view image in full size  
![][image3]

I had recently moved to the Bay Area post-college, bumming it at my parents’ place. This is important because I had been in NYC for the better part of five years, where owning a car was just the ramblings of a crazy person. Never in my life did I think that lil ol’ me would one day put my hands behind the death machine to and from work.

Somehow I became the crazy person. Starting my internship at Sensigo meant commuting from the East Bay to Redwood City. If you know that traffic, you know the hell I signed up for. I sat in my car, moving an inch every ten minutes, and thought, “He did not know how good he had it.”While painful, this commute inspired the project I was about to make, though at first it took a much different form.

## **The Image, Claude Code, and Credit Anxiety**

I saw a painterly beach-and-ocean image on are.na. I dropped it into Claude Code and asked for a React Three Fiber environment based on it.I’ll be honest, I’m not super familiar with React. But from using Figma Make, I noticed these tools are comfortable in a React framework, so I went with what felt familiar.

Press enter or click to view image in full size  
![][image4]  
*Matrix Study*, created in 1971 by the New Zealand surrealist artist Brent Wong.

The only problem is that I am not the most familiar with React.js, and especially React Three Fiber, so at the beginning there was the worry of debugging. If something were to happen where I needed to shift from building to finding an error, then I would be screwed into wasting credits. Especially since I was using Claude Opus 4.5, where it feels like you are playing Russian roulette on when your credits will run up.I see the appeal. There’s an exhilaration when a prompt turns into a scene. What used to take me 3 to 4 days of docs, Stack Overflow, and Reddit now happens in minutes. You can make whatever you want in seconds, I thought.

Just to preface, I’m a designer building a small Three.js scene, so this might not translate to traditional projects. That said, here’s what I noticed while vibecoding 3D.

## **Every Scene Is Lit Like a Netflix Movie**

I don’t really set scenes up from scratch anymore thanks to AI, and it’s nice skipping the tedious Three.js setup. But a common issue is that no matter the program, everything ends up lit the same.The GitHub projects it references tend to share the same basic setup, which makes everything look identical. For me, that’s a big issue because lighting is the main driver of narrative.

Press enter or click to view image in full size  
![][image5]  
The output I got from my Claude prompt

Unlike traditional 2D interfaces where you use Gestalt principles in order to create hierarchy and experience, it is a much different story in 3D programming. Lighting creates a mood, whether it is the harsh top-down light of noon or a low, warm edge light that reads as dusk. What elevates 3D interfaces from 2D experiences is the cinematic aspect that you can create, because many 3D programs unfortunately lack this skill in favor of fluid animation or realistic models. I am not saying those are not important. It is just something I have noticed: lighting is not really used for signification purposes, only to really focus on more aesthetics.

Automation helps, but it comes with biases baked in. Code is not apolitical, and the idea that a prompt can recreate what is in your head is a fiction. Those aesthetic choices are not glitches, they are the foundation, and they get louder as the models advance.

Something that became common for me while using AI on 3D projects was making everything adjustable. Doing that by hand would be a chore, but a live control panel let me un-AI the scene and make it feel more human.

## **How To Push Against The Biases**

When the Opus credits ran out, I went to the terminal. It sounds advanced, but I really only know two commands. You can drag your scene folder in and run whatever CLI AI app you want. With Leva panels set up, I do most of the visual debugging there and leave the logic to the AI.

![Become a member][image7]

I punch above my weight by pointing the AI at GitHub repos. It can reuse known setups instead of starting from scratch. For PS1, it handled dithering, posterization, and low-res scaling, and I could tweak them live. The only thing it missed was the classic jitter, so I pulled that from a repo and put it in the shader.

That one image started to narrow my focus. I kept optimizing for resemblance, and everything else fell to the side. It turned into tunnel vision.Every tutorial you see on design channels and influencers pushes the same idea: AI can turn your live designs into code, bringing something static to life. It’s the Pinocchio effect, where designers go from luxury to necessity. Like Pinocchio saying he is a real boy, the designer says, “I can produce labor just like a programmer can.”

This purpose of AI is something I have no interest in. In fact, I was just about going to drop this project until the programs started to glitch out and I was left like a deer in headlights with no idea how to react.

![][image8]  
The glitching effect I got the further I got.

## **Make Mistakes Great Again**

To save you time, after yelling at the AI in Caps Lock, I figured it out through the Leva sliders: it had added a custom post-processing shader pass. It handled posterization, dithering, bloom, vignette, and grain, which made the scene painterly before I layered the PS1 effects. This is what it looked like before the fixes.

I spent a lot of time trying to find the issue, and that forced me to sit with the scene. I tweaked the sliders and took screenshots. Leva put all the camera controls in one place. When I went isometric, the ortho camera locked onto a target and left me zoomed into the mountain. I kept fiddling with post-processing and took a few shots.

![][image9]  
Press enter or click to view image in full size  
![][image10]

As I zoomed out, the camera unlocked and I drifted outside the scene into the sky dome. That fake space view on a laptop screen made me think about my relationship with the internet and how it creates its own time and space.I kept thinking about myself in that car on the highway, boxed in by other cars, inch by inch on a cool Bay Area night. But I’m not in the car. I’m looking from the outside through an isometric camera in Three.js. I zoom out, headlights smear. I zoom out again and it’s just me alone on the earth, driving to nowhere.

## **Zooming Out and Focusing**

Coming back into the picture, my final vision started to form, unexpected but perfect. From that reflection, I realized I wanted to make an experience about the global commute, with all its small pleasures and annoyances.

Press enter or click to view image in full size  
![][image12]

Creating a space around my ideas of time, I built a custom sky dome and used real-world sun math to keep it believable. I take a location (manual, Tokyo by default, or auto via geolocation with an IP fallback), read the local timezone, and compute sun azimuth and altitude from the date and lat/long. Those values drive the sky gradient and the directional light, updating every second so the scene stays synced to real time.

I wanted a calming overwhelm, and I wanted the road to feel endless in either direction. But I still wanted the sky to stay visible. So the scene lives inside a world-space reveal mask that follows the player, using fragment shaders to discard pixels outside a circular radius while leaving the sky untouched. The mask even draws a ring outline so I can see it.I was too lost in the AI sauce, so I kept asking it to fix this for me. No matter how many curse words and Caps Lock I threw out, nothing stuck. It felt like another boundary the AI could not cross, so I shelved it and started loading assets.

Press enter or click to view image in full size  
![][image13]  
Press enter or click to view image in full size  
![][image14]

Keeping the PS1 style, I used low-poly assets, starting with the road. I imported it, dropped it in, and told Claude to wire it up. The road is a single GLB segment repeated around the player to feel infinite, and I can adjust its scale, spacing, and rotation live. And just like that, it worked, pretty much perfectly. I was almost shocked.I felt a little guilty building this. If you asked me to explain the code, I could not. It became something unknown and complicated, but it worked, and isn’t that what matters?

## **The Final Touches**

I had Claude set up most of the assets. The lesson was obvious: expect AI mistakes, and build your own safety net. Mine was the Leva panel. It got as messy as a 15-page essay due the night before, but it was the only way I could keep creative control.

Press enter or click to view image in full size  
![][image15]

Every model had its axis, position, and rotation adjustable. I could treat the environment more like Blender than code. The car physics were tunable too: acceleration, steering return, grip, drag, even suspension bob. It made the motion feel smooth instead of robotic.That is how I got the environment exactly where I wanted it. Even the lighting position was customizable, pushing it away from the drab Netflix-esque look. The last thing left was the reveal-mask shader. Since prompting didn’t get me there, I had to do my own research and map out the logic.It is… It is… Beautifulll\!\!\!

Upon completing the project Sunday night, I couldn’t help but procrastinate. I just kept driving with music in the background. It’s embarrassing to admit, but it felt like therapy not having to deal with shifting levels of traffic. I could flow across the road as fast or as slow as I wanted, all under my control.

Designing is essential, but it is embarrassing how many digital experience designers cannot code. It feels like an odd exception in design, because print and furniture designers still publish and build their work. Only UX designers seem to get the privilege of not building.That’s why the excitement for these tools feels weird. Yes, you can build apps with them, but you will hit a wall. And no matter how many times you ask the AI to explain it like you’re five, you will still be confused. That pain point will take time to go away.

Press enter or click to view image in full size  
![][image16]  
The scene in different times of day

The only real solution is to learn how products are built. It may feel boring, but a concept can only go so far. It is through building and feeling the product that you understand it. Figma screens and ProtoPie prototypes cannot reflect frame pacing, input latency, or post-processing costs in a shader-heavy scene.But the experience of AI coding, intentional or not, does not leave much space to reflect. Once you feel that periodic dopamine rush of creating, you will endure the mistakes.But I think there’s something interesting if you reframe it. Those mistakes can become points of reflection. Working with the machine, instead of treating it as a mistake, it becomes a space where biases can be seen, manipulated, and rewritten.
